q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in their WHERE clause conditions. Q1 requires X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3, which implies all three columns are equal (transitive equality). Q2 requires X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3, which also implies all three columns are equal. However, when NULL values are involved, the behavior differs because NULL = NULL returns NULL (not TRUE), so a row where A1, A2, and A3 are all NULL will be filtered out by both queries since the conditions evaluate to NULL (treated as FALSE). But if only two columns are NULL and equal, while the third is a different value (or NULL but not all three NULL), the conditions may evaluate differently. Specifically, if A1 and A2 are NULL (so A1 = A2 is NULL) and A3 is not NULL, then Q1's condition (NULL AND NULL = A3) is NULL (FALSE), and Q2's condition (NULL AND NULL = A3) is also NULL (FALSE), so no difference. The key difference arises when the columns are not all equal and NULLs break the transitivity. For example, if A1 = 1, A2 = 1, A3 = NULL: Q1 checks (A1=A2 is TRUE) AND (A2=A3 is NULL) → NULL (FALSE), so row excluded. Q2 checks (A1=A2 is TRUE) AND (A1=A3 is NULL) → NULL (FALSE), so row excluded—same result. To find a counterexample, consider A1 = 1, A2 = NULL, A3 = 1: Q1 checks (A1=A2 is NULL) AND (A2=A3 is NULL) → NULL (FALSE), excluded. Q2 checks (A1=A2 is NULL) AND (A1=A3 is TRUE) → NULL (FALSE), excluded—same. The real divergence occurs when the conditions evaluate to TRUE in one query and FALSE/NULL in the other. This happens if A1 = A2 but A2 ≠ A3 and A1 = A3, which is impossible since equality is transitive. Thus, under strict equality and NULL handling, Q1 and Q2 are equivalent because both require A1 = A2 and A1 = A3 (and hence A2 = A3). Therefore, no counterexample exists under the given schema without additional constraints.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2, A3) VALUES (1, 1, 1); -- Both queries return this row. No INSERTs can make the queries output different results as they are equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists because both queries are logically equivalent: Q1 requires A1 = A2 and A2 = A3, which implies A1 = A3 (transitivity of equality), so it is equivalent to Q2 which requires A1 = A2 and A1 = A3. Even with NULL values, the conditions behave identically since any NULL comparison returns NULL, and both queries filter out rows where any of the equalities is NULL.
